Profile likelihood

Source: vignettes/articles/methods-profiles.Rmd
methods-profiles.Rmd

The profile likelihood gives confidence intervals of parameters and predictions of nonlinear models without a quadratic approximation [1], [2]. Guide: Profile likelihood, Prediction uncertainty.

Profile and threshold

The objective function \(\ell(\theta) = -2 \log L(\theta) - 2 \log \pi(\theta)\) is the data term \(-2 \log L\) plus the prior term \(-2 \log \pi\) of the prior \(\pi\) (Likelihood and prior). normL2() returns the data term as attribute data, constraintL2() the prior term as prior, and profile() keeps both as columns. The profile of \(\theta_i\) is \(\ell\) minimized over all other parameters as a function of \(\theta_i = c\). The minimizing values of the other parameters form the parameter path \(\hat\theta(c)\),

\[\hat\theta(c) = \operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\theta \,:\, \theta_i = c}\, \ell(\theta) , \tag{1}\]

and the profile likelihood is the objective along this path,

\[\mathrm{PL}_i(c) = \ell\bigl(\hat\theta(c)\bigr) . \tag{2}\]

A parameter that moves with \(\theta_i\) along the path compensates the change of \(\theta_i\) in the predictions (plotPaths()).

Without a prior, (2) is the minimum of \(-2 \log L\) with \(\theta_i = c\). By the likelihood ratio test, the rise \(\mathrm{PL}_i(c) - \mathrm{PL}_i(\hat\theta_i)\) from the optimum \(\hat\theta_i\) below the threshold, the \(1 - \alpha\) quantile of \(\chi^2_1\) (3.84 for 95 %), defines an asymptotic confidence interval, the set of values \(c\) compatible with the data, invariant under reparameterization of \(\theta_i\). The optimum is the minimum of (2). profileThreshold() computes the threshold, method = "F" the finite-sample threshold \(n \log(1 + F_{1,\nu,1-\alpha}/\nu)\) with \(n\) data points and \(\nu = n - p\) for \(p\) estimated mean parameters, exact for Gaussian errors with one estimated standard deviation. A prior wide against the data curvature keeps (1) finite where the data do not determine \(\theta_i\) and changes (2) little where they do.

profile() stops on (2) by default; stepControl = list(stop = "data") ends a profile at the threshold of the data term \(-2 \log L\bigl(\hat\theta(c)\bigr)\) along the path, and confint(val.column = "data") reads the interval off that term.

Shapes

A parameter is identifiable when (2) exceeds the threshold on both sides, otherwise non-identifiable: practically non-identifiable when the profile stays below the threshold on one side or both for the given data, structurally non-identifiable when different parameter values give the same prediction of every observable and the profile is flat (Structural identifiability). A symmetry is a transformation of the parameters that leaves every observable unchanged; a gauge fixes coordinates so that each orbit of the symmetry meets the fixed values in one point (Gauge and reduction).

shape of (2) meaning
above the threshold on both sides finite interval
below the threshold on one side practically non-identifiable
exactly flat structurally non-identifiable, a symmetry (Symmetries), removed by a gauge

On the log scale, a one-sided profile towards \(-\infty\) means the reaction can be switched off, towards \(+\infty\) that the process is in equilibrium on the time scale of the data, replaceable by a large fixed value or the quasi-steady state. Both limits give a reduced model, the model with the parameter at the limit, with the same fit [3]. Each profile tests one limit with all other parameters free; several limits together need a likelihood ratio test of the reduced model.

Computing a profile

A profile is a sequence of constrained fits, each started from the last point.

  • method = "optimize" steps \(\theta_i\) and refits the others with trust(), one converged fit per point.

  • method = "integrate", the integration-based profile, follows the constrained optimum \(\hat\theta(c)\) of (1), the stationary point of the Lagrangian \(\ell(\theta) + \lambda\,(\theta_i - c)\), where \(\nabla \ell + \lambda e_i = 0\) and \(\theta_i = c\). Differentiating in \(c\) gives the path equation, the linear system for \(\mathrm{d}\theta/\mathrm{d}c\) that the profile follows in Euler steps,

    \[\begin{pmatrix} H & e_i \\ e_i^\top & 0 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \mathrm{d}\theta/\mathrm{d}c \\ \mathrm{d}\lambda/\mathrm{d}c \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} \tag{3}\]

    with the Hessian \(H\) of \(\ell\): one evaluation and one linear solve per step. The step solves (3) with \(-\gamma \nabla \ell\) in place of the upper zero, which pulls it back to the constrained optimum (\(\gamma = 1\) by default, adapted to the size of the pull). With a Gauss-Newton \(H\) the path still drifts, so each step is then corrected by a short fit of the other parameters with trust(), at most optControl$iterlim = 10 iterations; algoControl = list(reoptimize = FALSE) leaves out the fit.

Step control and stops:

rule setting
step shrinks mismatch of predicted and actual change above atol
step doubles mismatch below 0.3 * atol, or below 0.3 * rtol relative
side ends objective (or data term, stop = "data") up by the threshold; limits relative to the optimum reached; limit steps

A point of \(\ell\) below the start value is a better optimum: fit and profiles are then to be repeated from it. Where the curvature jumps, the step shrinks to min and stays on the profile.

Prediction profiles

A prediction \(z = g(t, \theta)\) has the prediction profile likelihood, the objective minimized under the constraint \(g(t, \theta) = z\),

\[\begin{aligned} \mathrm{PPL}(z) &= \ell\bigl(\hat\theta(z)\bigr) , \\ \hat\theta(z) &= \operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\theta \,:\, g(t, \theta) = z}\, \ell(\theta) , \end{aligned} \tag{4}\]

whose threshold gives a confidence interval of the prediction [2], over several \(t\) a pointwise confidence band. Without a prior the interval is the image of the parameter region at the \(\chi^2_1\) threshold, the set of \(\theta\) with \(-2 \log L\) less than 3.84 above the minimum, not of the joint region, which uses the \(\chi^2_p\) quantile of all \(p\) parameters at once and is larger.

A validation data point, a hypothetical measurement \(v\) of the prediction with standard deviation \(\sigma_v\), makes \(z\) a parameter \(v\), tied to the prediction by

\[\left( \frac{g(t, \theta) - v}{\sigma_v} \right)^2 . \tag{5}\]

The validation profile, the profile of \(v\), is (4) for \(\sigma_v \to 0\) and lies below (4) otherwise. The interval of \(v\), the range of a new measurement compatible with model and data, is therefore wider: for a quadratic (4) of half-width \(w\) the half-width becomes \((w^2 + \Delta \sigma_v^2)^{1/2}\), \(\Delta\) the threshold. datapointL2() builds (5) as an objfn from the evaluation of normL2(), which therefore predicts at \(t\) (times = t). With attrName = "data", (5) adds to the data term, so stop = "data" and confint(val.column = "data") include it. Where the model cannot follow \(v\), (5) grows and ends the profile.

[2]
C. Kreutz, A. Raue, and J. Timmer, “Likelihood based observability analysis and confidence intervals for predictions of dynamic models,” BMC Systems Biology, vol. 6, no. 1, p. 120, 2012, doi: 10.1186/1752-0509-6-120.
[3]
T. Maiwald et al., “Driving the model to its limit: Profile likelihood based model reduction,” PLOS ONE, vol. 11, no. 9, p. e0162366, 2016, doi: 10.1371/journal.pone.0162366.
